Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

ISLAMABAD, Pakistan (CNN) -- Eight cadets and staff members were killed in Pakistan during an an eight-hour standoff Monday with gunmen who stormed a police training center in Lahore, said Gen. Athar Abbas, a military spokesman. Police fire into the air after retaking the police training center in Lahore attacked by militants. The militants had been holed up on the top floor of a three-story building, said Rehman Malik, the head of the country's Interior Ministry. Security forces gained control of the first two floors and eventually made their way to the top, finally taking control of it and arresting the gunmen Monday afternoon. Television pictures showed security forces firing into the air from the roof of the building after the firefight. "The operation is over. Four terrorists were killed and three arrested," Interior Ministry Secretary Kamal Shah told Reuters. Malik and Abbas confirmed the figures. Abbas added some of the dead militants blew themselves up. The gang of seven gunmen stormed the academy in the Manawan area of the eastern Pakistani city, said Malik. Abbas had previously said 30 people were killed. He cited the error on wrong information by his sources at the scene.  Watch more about the attack » . At a news conference Monday night, Malik named the leader of the Pakistani Taliban, Baitullah Mehsud, and his followers as the prime suspect in organizing the attack. Mehsud is also accused of plotting the assassination of former PM Benazir Bhutto. At least 78 people were wounded in the attack, authorities said. Lahore is the same city where gunmen opened fire March 10 on a bus carrying members of the Sri Lankan national cricket team on their way to a stadium for a match. The well-coordinated attack wounded at least eight members of the team and killed a driver and six Pakistani police officers. In Monday's incident, the attackers hurled grenades, then stormed the compound and opened fire while officers were taking part in their morning drill. About 800 officers train at the facility, but authorities could not say exactly how many were inside at the time. The attackers, some in police uniforms, took dozens of officers hostage, said Asim Rizwan, spokesman for governor of Punjab -- the province where Lahore is located. Paramilitary forces and the army descended on the scene. Every few minutes, the gunmen detonated explosives or fired on reporters and police personnel outside, sending them scurrying for cover. Angry onlookers pumped their fists in the air and cheered as police led away a suspect they had captured. He had on him a grenade and a knife, officials told CNN. CNN's Reza Sayah contributed to this report.

ISLAMABAD, Pakistan (CNN) — A Monday assault on a police training facility in Lahore, Pakistan, ended after an eight-hour confrontation with armed militants, leaving eight cadets and staff members dead, according to military spokesman Gen. Athar Abbas.

After security forces regained control of the Lahore police training center, officers fired their weapons into the air. Rehman Malik, who heads Pakistan’s Interior Ministry, said the attackers had barricaded themselves on the upper level of a three-story structure. Security personnel first secured the lower two floors, then advanced to the top floor, where they ultimately took control and detained the surviving gunmen Monday afternoon.

Television footage showed security forces standing on the roof and firing into the air following the gun battle.

“The operation is over. Four terrorists were killed and three arrested,” Interior Ministry Secretary Kamal Shah told Reuters. Malik and Abbas verified those numbers. Abbas also said that some of the militants who died had detonated explosives on themselves.

Malik said the assault was carried out by seven gunmen who entered the academy in Manawan, an area of Lahore in eastern Pakistan. Abbas had earlier reported that 30 people had died, but later said that figure was incorrect and had been based on inaccurate information from sources at the scene.

At a news conference Monday evening, Malik identified Pakistani Taliban leader Baitullah Mehsud and his supporters as the main suspects behind the attack. Mehsud has also been accused of involvement in the plot to assassinate former Prime Minister Benazir Bhutto.

Authorities said at least 78 people were injured.

The violence occurred in Lahore, the same city where gunmen attacked a bus on March 10 carrying Sri Lanka’s national cricket team to a stadium for a match. That organized assault injured at least eight team members and killed a driver along with six Pakistani police officers.

In Monday’s attack, the assailants first threw grenades before entering the compound and shooting as police officers were conducting their morning drill. Roughly 800 officers receive training at the center, though officials could not confirm exactly how many were present when the attack began.

Some of the attackers were dressed in police uniforms, said Asim Rizwan, a spokesman for the governor of Punjab province, where Lahore is located. He said the gunmen seized dozens of officers as hostages.

Paramilitary units and army forces then moved into the area. At intervals of a few minutes, the militants either set off explosives or shot at journalists and police outside the facility, forcing them to run for cover.

Crowds nearby reacted angrily but cheered and raised their fists as police escorted away one captured suspect. Officials told CNN the man was carrying a grenade and a knife.

CNN’s Reza Sayah contributed to the report.

The attack began when militants forced their way into the compound and opened fire on cadets and staff. Explosions and gunfire echoed through the building as the attackers moved inside, trapping many people and sparking panic among recruits undergoing training at the center. Security forces quickly surrounded the site, and a prolonged operation followed as commandos worked methodically to retake the building floor by floor.

By the time the standoff ended, eight police cadets and staff members had been killed and at least 78 others were wounded. Officials said four militants were killed during the operation, while three others were captured alive. The arrests were expected to provide investigators with information about who planned and supported the assault.

Pakistani officials identified Pakistani Taliban leader Baitullah Mehsud as the prime suspect behind the attack. Mehsud, already blamed for a number of major militant operations, was seen by authorities as one of the most dangerous extremist figures in the country.

The raid also raised urgent concerns about the security of police and military facilities, as well as the vulnerability of recruits and trainees. For many Pakistanis, the attack was another sign that the country’s internal security crisis was deepening, with militant groups willing and able to carry out coordinated attacks against state institutions.

counterfactuals.output:
**Militants storm police academy in Lahore, killing cadets and security personnel**

**LAHORE, Pakistan —** Militants armed with guns and grenades stormed a police training academy on the outskirts of Lahore on Monday, killing at least eight police recruits and security personnel and wounding dozens more in an hours-long siege that ended after Pakistani commandos retook the compound, officials said.

The attack began in the morning at the Manawan Police Training School, near Pakistan’s border with India, as hundreds of unarmed recruits were taking part in a parade or morning drill, police and witnesses said. Gunmen opened fire and threw grenades, sending cadets scrambling for cover as explosions and automatic gunfire echoed through the complex.

Pakistani security forces surrounded the academy and launched an operation to clear the buildings. Television footage showed commandos moving across rooftops and through the grounds, while some police recruits climbed walls or crawled through fields to escape.

Officials said several attackers were killed and others captured. Interior Ministry officials said authorities were questioning suspects and investigating possible links to Taliban and al Qaeda-linked militant networks operating in Pakistan’s tribal areas. Pakistani Taliban leader Baitullah Mehsud later claimed responsibility for the attack in some media reports, though officials said investigators were still working to confirm the full chain of command and whether other extremist groups were involved.

Pakistan’s then-interior adviser, Rehman Malik, said the attackers appeared to be highly trained and suggested the assault bore the hallmarks of organized militant groups seeking to destabilize the country. He said security agencies had recovered weapons and explosives from the scene and were examining the identities of the captured men.

“This was a planned terrorist attack,” Malik told reporters, saying the government would pursue those responsible.

Punjab officials condemned the assault and said the attackers targeted a symbol of law enforcement in an effort to undermine public confidence. Lahore had already been on edge after a high-profile attack earlier that month on the Sri Lankan cricket team, also in the city, which killed several police officers and wounded players.

The Manawan siege lasted roughly eight hours before security forces declared the academy cleared. Officials said dozens of injured recruits and officers were taken to nearby hospitals, some with serious gunshot and shrapnel wounds.

The attack underscored the growing reach of militant groups in Pakistan beyond the country’s northwest, where security forces were battling Taliban fighters. Lahore, Pakistan’s second-largest city and the capital of Punjab province, had increasingly become a target for militants striking government, security and foreign-linked sites.

Pakistani leaders vowed to continue operations against extremist networks, saying attacks on police and military facilities would not deter the state.

“This is a war against terrorism,” Malik said. “We will not bow before these terrorists.”

The academy attack came weeks after gunmen in Lahore ambushed the Sri Lankan national cricket team, killing police officers and wounding several players and officials. *Lahore, Pakistan* — Pakistani security forces stormed a police training academy on the outskirts of Lahore on Monday, ending an hours-long siege after gunmen attacked the compound, killed recruits and held off authorities in a battle that raised new concerns about militant violence in the country’s cultural capital.

After several hours, commandos launched a final operation to retake the building, clearing rooms and rooftops before declaring the compound back under government control.

Officials said multiple attackers were killed or captured, though early casualty figures varied. Authorities also reported deaths among police recruits and security personnel, with many others wounded.

That assault, which targeted the team’s convoy near the city’s Gaddafi Stadium, shocked the cricket world and led to renewed scrutiny of militant networks operating in Punjab province.

Investigators were examining whether the police academy attack bore operational similarities to the Sri Lankan team ambush, including the use of multiple gunmen, automatic weapons and a coordinated strike on a high-profile target in Lahore. No immediate definitive link was confirmed, but Pakistani officials said they were exploring possible connections between the two attacks.

The violence underscored the growing reach of militant groups beyond Pakistan’s tribal areas and northwest frontier regions, where the government has battled Taliban-linked fighters and other extremists. Lahore, Pakistan’s second-largest city, had increasingly become a target of major attacks, challenging official claims that urban centers remained secure.

CNN reported from Pakistan on the attack, with reporting and contributions from CNN correspondents and contributors in the region.
